title: EvoLM: In Search of Lost Language Model Training Dynamics

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.1, paragraph beginning 'Table 1 presents a filtered comparison...' (line 87)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper's own body text criticizes its own Table 1 evidence in the third person: 'Table 1 presents a filtered comparison favoring smaller models... The compute budget equivalence is thus misleading because training for more tokens on smaller models does not equate to the same compute expended on larger models with fewer tokens. Effective compute normalization accounting for FLOPs and step counts is absent, resulting in incomplete and cherry-picked evidence that exaggerates smaller models' competitive edge while underreporting larger models' potential.' This reads as embedded reviewer feedback rather than paper content, and it directly contradicts the paper's own framing two paragraphs later (line 96): 'under a fixed pre-training compute budget (1B–320BT vs. 4B–80BT), the smaller 1B model even outperforms the 4B model'. A paper asserting that its own central comparison is based on 'incomplete and cherry-picked evidence' is a conclusion-undermining self-contradiction that would require correction.

Section 4.1 criticizes its own paper in the third person: 'While Section 4.1 highlights limitations of intermediate checkpoints as proxies, Section 3 experiments rely extensively on such checkpoints for performance evaluation across token budgets. This conflicting usage suggests a methodological inconsistency that undermines conclusions drawn from intermediate checkpoint analysis.' This is self-invalidating text (Section 4.1 referring to itself as 'Section 4.1') and explicitly admits that Section 3's results, which are core to the paper's claims about scaling dynamics, are undermined by a methodological inconsistency. Such a statement — whether an embedded review note or deliberate — requires correction/removal and invalidates the reliability of the Section 3 analyses.

The Abstract states release is partial: 'we release selected pre-trained and post-trained models along with portions of the training datasets and partial evaluation scripts. However, due to proprietary portions of the dataset and internal infrastructure dependencies, full training pipelines and all data cannot be fully released publicly at this time.' The Introduction contribution bullet states full release: 'Open-sourcing 100+ LMs trained from scratch with 1B and 4B parameters and their training data for all stages, enabling the research community to build upon our findings.' 'All data for all stages' (full open-sourcing) is incompatible with 'full training pipelines and all data cannot be fully released.' The paper contradicts itself on the central open-source deliverable.

Table 1 is referenced three times in the main text ('Table 1 presents a filtered comparison favoring smaller models' line 87; 'As Table 1 illustrates' line 96; 'This is also reflected by results in Table 1' line 200) but no Table 1 is defined or displayed anywhere in the paper. The appendix contains Table 4 (observational comparison) and Tables 5-9, but no Table 1 caption or table body exists. The claimed data underlying the 1B-320BT vs 4B-80BT comparison is therefore unavailable for verification.

The appendix describes 'FineMath [38]' attributing the dataset to reference [38] = Penedo et al., 'The FineWeb Datasets' (the FineWeb paper). FineMath is a mathematical pretraining dataset introduced in the SmolLM2 technical report (Allal et al., arXiv:2502.02737), not in the FineWeb paper. Web verification confirms FineMath originates with the SmolLM2/FineMath release (HuggingFaceTB/finemath). Moreover, the main text (Section 2.1, line 45) correctly cites FineMath as [2] (SmolLM2). The same dataset is therefore attributed to two different references, one of which ([38]) is the wrong paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 7 caption (b) (line 196) vs Section 3.4 'Varying RL dataset size' (line 202)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text says 'Varying RL dataset size. Given a fixed epoch of 8, we vary the RL dataset size from 0 to 400K examples.' But the Figure 7 caption describes these models as '1B-160BT-8+42BT-100K-ep1-{0, 50K, 100K, 150K, ..., 400K}-ep1', where the trailing '-ep1' (following the paper's naming convention of Section 2.1: '{SFT examples}Kep{SFT epochs}-{RL examples}Kep{RL epochs}') specifies RL training for 1 epoch, not 8. The caption and text disagree on the fixed RL epoch count for the dataset-size sweep.

The body states RL peaks/saturates at 'around 8–16 epochs' (line 200) and that gains 'continue to increase from more data up to around 150–200K examples' (line 202). Takeaway 9 states 'saturation happens at 4–8 epochs or 50–100K examples in our study'. The reported saturation points differ on both axes (8–16 vs 4–8 epochs; 150–200K vs 50–100K examples) between the takeaway and the results it summarizes.

predicted_errors.error_location: Appendix A.1 text (line 478) vs Table 4 (rows '1B (ours) 320B' and '4B (ours) 320B')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims 'our 1B and 4B models achieve similar or slightly better results across standard benchmarks' relative to TinyLlama-1B and Qwen1.5-4B. Table 4 shows the opposite: the 1B-320B model averages 52.49 vs TinyLlama-1B's 53.23 (ours lower), and the 4B-320B model averages 56.94 vs Qwen1.5-4B's 58.86 (ours lower). On every individual benchmark listed, the EvoLM models are slightly worse, so 'similar or slightly better' overstates the comparison and is contradicted by the paper's own table.

References [4] (Bethune et al., Scaling Laws for Forgetting), [39] (Qi et al., Mutual Reasoning Makes Smaller LLMs Stronger Problem-Solvers), and [62] (Yildiz et al., Investigating Continual Pre-training) appear in the bibliography but are never cited anywhere in the main text or appendix. A programmatic scan of the full paper (excluding the bibliography block) confirms zero in-text references to [4], [39], or [62]. These are dangling bibliography entries.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.4, 'Varying RL dataset size' paragraph (lines 202 vs 214)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Line 202 describes the 350K/400K example performance drops as an open question tied to 'unreported training instabilities, such as excessive sequence lengths exceeding model context windows and insufficient truncation policies. Additional training diagnostics are needed to confirm whether these drops reflect model failures or experimental artifacts.' Line 214 then asserts the cause as established fact: 'Training results show that during the final RL steps, both models learn to greatly increase response length, and their generations often exceed their predefined context-window lengths, causing the performance drop.' The text contradicts itself on whether the cause is confirmed or speculative, and the phrase 'unreported training instabilities' is an admission that a reported result rests on undocumented training issues.

The tables presented for Figure 5 and Figure 6 do not contain per-metric data values. In the Figure 5 table the four metric columns (Greedy, Maj@16, RM@16, Pass@16) are populated with identical sequences for both the ID and OOD rows ('0.5 0.4 0.3 0.2' and '0.6 0.5 0.4 0.3'), the ORM column contains '5.0 7.5 10.0 12.5 15.0', and the Correct Ratio column '0.35 0.30 0.25 0.20 0.15' — all consistent with matplotlib axis tick labels rather than actual measurements. Identical values across four distinct metrics are implausible for real data, and the 'Epochs' row ('4 8 16 32') contains x-axis values. The table therefore provides no verifiable data values for the Figure 5/6 claims; at best this is a severe presentation error that makes the underlying results unverifiable.

Section 2.1 states CPT token budgets 'ranging from 2B to 42B'. Section 3.2 states 'varying the total CPT tokens from 0 (no CPT) to 50 BT' and Table 2 includes the configuration 'FineMath 50BT'. A FineMath-only budget of 50B tokens exceeds the stated 2B-42B upper bound. Either the stated range or the 50BT experiment is inconsistent.

Line 71 hedges the central saturation result: 'Confidence intervals would reveal considerable fluctuations around 80x to 160x model size, suggesting the apparent saturation may partly reflect noise rather than definitive plateauing', and admits 'notable run-to-run variability is not shown'. Takeaway 1 states the opposite as definitive: 'Excessive pre-training can lead not only to diminishing returns but also to degradation in downstream generalization, particularly on OOD tasks.' A result whose saturation 'may partly reflect noise' is presented elsewhere as a firm finding of degradation.

The Introduction states 'Pre-trained on publicly available corpora FineWeb [38] only', while the Methods section states 'Pre-training: Conducted exclusively on FineWeb-Edu [38]' and the appendix likewise describes 'FineWeb-Edu [38]'. FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu are distinct corpora (Edu is a filtered educational subset of FineWeb). The paper uses the two names interchangeably for its pretraining corpus across sections.

The paper identifies the best-performing replay configuration as 8 BT replay + 42 BT FineMath (Table 2: 21.01% vs 19.27% for pure FineMath), then calls this 'a modest replay budget (around 5%)' (line 108) and recommends 'a small replay budget (e.g., 5%)' (Takeaway 3). As a fraction of the 50 BT CPT mix, 8 BT is 16%, not ~5%. The 'around 5%' figure only holds as a fraction of the 160 BT pretraining corpus (8/160), which is not the quantity being discussed in the CPT context.

summary: The EvoLM paper (17950) was segmented into 40 snippets (16 sections, 10 tables, 14 figures) and verified in exhaustive mode at lenient strictness. Fifteen predicted errors were found, several of high confidence. The most serious are three passages of embedded reviewer-style self-critique that invalidate the paper's own findings: Section 3.1 describes its Table 1 evidence as 'incomplete and cherry-picked', Section 4.1 admits Section 3's reliance on intermediate checkpoints 'undermines conclusions', and Section 3.4 references 'unreported training instabilities' while elsewhere asserting the cause of a reported performance drop as established fact. The Abstract (partial release) contradicts the Introduction contribution bullet (full open-sourcing of '100+ LMs... and their training data for all stages'). Table 1 is referenced three times but never appears. The RL dataset-size sweep is internally inconsistent (Figure 7 caption specifies 1 RL epoch vs the text's fixed 8 epochs; Takeaway 9's saturation points of 4-8 epochs / 50-100K examples conflict with the body's 8-16 epochs / 150-200K examples). FineMath is misattributed to the FineWeb paper ([38]) in Appendix B.2.3 while correctly cited as [2] in the main text, and references [4], [39], [62] are dangling. The claim that EvoLM models achieve 'similar or slightly better' results than TinyLlama/Qwen1.5 is contradicted by the paper's own Table 4 (both EvoLM models are slightly worse). The Figure 5/6 tables contain only axis-tick labels rather than data values. Given multiple high-confidence, conclusion-invalidating inconsistencies, the paper requires correction.
